newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN anxious about Rwandans stranded in Zaire, Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: UN anxious about Rwandans stranded in Zaire, Tanzania.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency expressed concern on Tuesday about more than 330,000 Rwandan refugees still stranded in eastern Zaire, especially 120,000 in a camp short of food and thought to be dominated by thugs.
Eleven to 15 people were dying every day at the Tingi Tingi camp, where food shortages had prompted conflict between the refugees and local Zaireans, spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said.
Most of the victims were young men.
Diarrhoea was rife in the camp, but there were no epidemics, according to the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

"Our staff there say the camp...has an unusually high proportion of young single males some of whom are likely to be Interahamwe (Hutu militia) or ex FAR (Rwandan army)," O'Toole told a news briefing in Geneva.

"Again the Tingi Tingi camp follows previous patterns -- many of these young men appear to be controlling the refugees' actions. Those people who have approached our staff asking about repatriation have done so secretly, as if scared of reprisals."

A 19-strong UNHCR team has set up an office in Kisangani to begin coordinating aid for refugees in eastern Zaire, located in several major clusters, including Tingi Tingi east of Lubutu, at Amisi (accommodating about 60,000 people) and south around the Shabunda area (150,000 people), the spokeswoman added.
"This does not mean that we have located and accounted for all of the refugees -- for instance yesterday some 4,500 emerged from a previously unknown location northwest of Bukavu."
UNHCR may try to open land corridors to bring supplies to the refugees in eastern Zaire, although this would involve crossing a war zone, O'Toole said.

"We don't want to simply set up permanent camps in this area -- this would simply be prolonging an already long-term problem. We must look for ways of separating the intimidators from genuine refugees," she said.

Some 719,307 Rwandans, mainly Hutus who fled in fear of reprisals after the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus, returned home from Zaire last year, according to the Geneva-based agency.

O'Toole also said the UNHCR was in high-level talks with authorities in Tanzania about Rwandans still in that country, and the agency wanted to set up a screening process to assess whether the refugees wanted to return home or seek asylum.
Noting that the Tanzanian government has said only small concentrations of Rwandans remain after more than 480,000 Rwandan refugees returned home in a one-month period, she added:
"We have had information that several hundred a day are still coming forward.

"Tanzania has given reassurances that those who do not want to go back will not be forced. We would like to see some kind of screening process set up for these remaining people who held back from the general repatriation."
